A scene of violence and disorder without any recent parallel occurred in the house of Commons on Mcnday, when the Lords' amendment, to the Veto Bill came nominally under consideration. When the House met, the grail'', of ti n crisis bad a trendy manifested itself in other and significant ways. OUTBREAK OF THE STORM.

The disturbance began the appearance of the Prime Minister at questi, n time. Up to that pint the crowded House lied indulged in gcod-ustured chaff bandied across the floor while private members were interrogating Ministers. Then Mr. Asquith stood for a moment behind the Speaker's chair. As soon as he was seen, the Liberals sprang to their feet, cheering and waving hats. The Tories uttered shouts of Traitor' as Mr. Asquith made his way to the seat opposite the dispatch b r. The Liberals cheered down their o. ponents. but again the shouts of " Traitor " burst forth, and the Speaker, rising calmly made an appeal—the first of many—to niembera to control themselves. Mr. isalLur, coming in a few minutes Liter, was also cheered by his party—but some of his followers rose reluctantly, and oiw or two tuutiLeers refused to acknowledge him. THE GENTLEMANLY PARTY.

The Prime Minister, turning to face the gentleman'y party, I egan his first sentence in calor, deliberate tones. The storm broke before he could complete it 'rho House rang with coherent and incoherent cries of insult ; but above them was heard the thin voice of Lord Pugh Cecil, crying inceseantly, " 'Vide! 'Vide!" Lord Castlereagh, Mr. Mitchell-Thomson, Mr. Goulding, and Major Archer-Slue, Mr. Remnant, ad several others took their turn at giving new epithets, and so the disgraceful scenes went on.

Presently the Speaker emit,' a momentary respite, and Mr. At:quith began his first sentence afresh. By this time it wan too evident that the Opposition meant to prevent the Premier from speaking. Lord Hugh's chant of "'Vide! 'Vide ' " went un incessantly. Mr Will Crooks told the House ho had known men certified " for less. But even Mr. Crooks could not bring the House back to g,xl humour. The tannta burled at the Pt ime Ilinhder it eluded " Patrick Ford " ; and, pointing to Mr. John Redmond, they shcuted, the Dictator spcsk ; we'll listen to Lint."

div.head: "WHO KILLED THE KING P'
div.p: "WHO KILLED THE KING P'

At one of the stormiest momenta Mr. F. E. Smith asked, " When the Prime ilit.ister has degraded the political life of the country, are we not entitled to"— the rest was net in shouts of " I lrder " as the Speaker rose to again appeal for the decencies of debate. lie had already pointed out to the Tories that it was to their interest to preserve order, because they were in the minority, and freedom of debate wee of importance to them, but this was disrcgirded. At la•t the Prime Minister contrived to be heard for some consecutive sentences. Ile began reviewing the events that have led to the present crisis, and when be rrmarked that the death of King Edward had brought about a truce, thrre was a shout of •• Who leilltd the King " from the Opposition beaches.

div.head: WOULD NOT LISTEN.
div.p: WOULD NOT LISTEN.

The Prime Miuister, having fought n ith beasts at Ephesus for about there-quarters of an hour, at last declared that he would not degrade himself by bandying words with members who muld not listen to him But in one short sentence he put the central fact before the Opposition. Ile drclaird that if the If. use if Lords would not accept the Bill of the Government sub,dantislly with, if thry liked, reason- able amendments, the Government would be compelled to invoke the r xercise of the Royal Prerogative. There wan one notable clause in the speech. abort Slut was. " There is trill time," Mr Asquith raid, dealing with the Peers' opportunity to introduce real and not wrecking amendments.

div.head: U. BALFOUR MEETS WITH COURTESY.
div.p: U. BALFOUR MEETS WITH COURTESY.

Mr. Balfour, rising t, reply, was met not with the expected counter-demonstration, hut with attentive nilence, for which Mr. Asquith wive the signal to his followers. NI r. Balfour expressed hie regret that the Prime Minister had not keen beard, and then plunged into a violent attack on the Government's use c the prerogative—as unconstitutional, unprecedented, 4' dragging the Crown ia the dust," and all for pre- venting the people from exp., s.ing their opinion on Home Rule. But Mr. Balfour gave the ta,..vernment credit for posti oning the ahnouncement ab.ut the luarantees until after the Corona,ion, out of deference, he buggeeted, to tl.e feelings of the Monarch. The only hint Mr. ltalfour gave ci hM own action on the crisis was to siy that the deci:inn must be revel sel l!ter vn

div.head: SIR EDWARD GREY'S REBUKE.
div.p: SIR EDWARD GREY'S REBUKE.

Sir Edward Grey gave a toudi of dignity t 3 tie final wanes. He told the Opputition that if they would Lot listen to the arguroeida of the Prime Minister no one of his suppotters would consent to take his place. He moved the adjournment if the House, and a few minutes later, when Mr. F. E. Smith had provoked a new outbreak of disorder, the Spn.dier exercised his authority under the St .nding Ordele in case r.l •• grave diawder," and declared the Kitting at an end.

div.head: EL ASQUITH'S SPEECH.
div.p: EL ASQUITH'S SPEECH.

lir. Asquith handed the notes of the speech he intended making in the Home of Commons to the Tram. Ile argued that the Parliament Bill had Teesised the deliberate and aFeeific sanction of the electors It twO general eLetien., that the Lansdowne

amendments were equivalent to a rejection of the pi ineiple of the Bill, and that in recommending the Crown to have ri.• •.rse to the creation of peers he wee following do. ••e lent set fry Lord Grey in 1832.

div.head: PERSONAL ATTACK.
div.p: A PERSONAL ATTACK.
TORIES ORGANISED VULGARITY.

In the " Morning Leader " Mr. Harold Spender comments ou the outbredt as follows The scene in the House of Commons will stand out iu history not no an outburst of dramatic passion, but ias an organised exhibition of incredible vulgarity and nudeness.

There WWI neither wit nor cleverness in this demonstration of regimented ,utlinisos If lifted the veil once and for all from those pretensions to"manners- that have been put forward by the people who are supposed to be represented by the Tories in the !louse of Commons. We know now, at any rate, who are

Nor Tin: 01,11.E111N ~F SI., The zurst dramatic thing about the afternoon:indeed was the coottaat between the behaviour of the Tories and the Liberals. Rarely in the history of Parliament has a great party behaved with greater self-restraint than that behind the Government on Monday after- noon. Remember that the members of that party are not only middle-class Liberals, but Labour men and Irishmen, who are supposed to stand outside the pale of drawing-ri out culture. The rougheet Labour man in the Rouse allowed up as the finest knight of chivalry iu contrast with the B,lls of dukes and peers sitting on the benches opposite. And let it not be forgotten that, whil, the British aristrcrscy gave itself up to an exhibition of unrestrained temper that would have been digraceful ins nursery. the Irishmen, who sat in serried rows on the benches behind them, were held by a perfect discipline. A PERSONAL ATTACK.

But still the wont thing ithnut it all remains, that it was organised, and that it was personal. , The org misers were Mr. Goulding, Mr. F. E Smith, • and Lord Hugh Cecil, who, it seems, have taken the greatest trouble about thin display, and consider it in ' proud achievement. Perhaps they will discover within a few weeks what the better mind of the House of Commons thinks of thew things. It was noticeable on Monday afternoon Hint when Mr. F. E. Smith rose and attempted to secure a hearing not a voice was raised on Ids behalf, even among his staunchest ' supporters on the her cl.es round him. It was felt that the organiser of disorder was meeting his deserin. Anti all this was directed against Mr. Asquith. dm most courteous and least provocative of Prime Ministers, amen of measuted and quiet spnech, who has given to none of these hooligans a shadow of an excuse for their In havi.mr.

The most signific-a-n.; thing aLout the whole affair watt the podtion of Mr. Baifour. Some of the Front Opposition Bona, notably Mr. Austen Chamberlsio, occasionally even encouraged the dis rder. But Mr. Balfour gave no sign. Ile sit with his head low down and Ids eyes cLsed, a picture tf human misery.

div.head: SPIRITED DEFENCE OF HOME
div.p: SPIRITED DEFENCE OF HOME
RULE

There was another large and enthosismic meeting at Bridge Foot on Monfley evening, tinder the auspices of the Progreasive Labour League. Mr. T. M. Evans, of Liverpool, aa• the chief speaker sad devoted his address niainly toe spirited exposition and defence of Home Ride. Mr. E. A. Sanders presided and ma. accompanied on thenlatf °rot by Mr. J. Morton and Mr. Harry Neve.

--The Cit itittisc said that at present the progressives bad everything on their side. In the House of Commons t hut afternoon the Opposition bed attempted to hound down the Prime Minister, but such tactics were only adopted by the doomed. (Applause). They wished to allay their eutTerings a little by not hearing their sentence. (Laughter., Ile expected the crisis eould pass without the creation ot new Peers, though that procedure would loot do any if onto, harm. It would in fact curtail I the powers of the Prior for ever, sod every Liberal measure that WII9 sent up to the Home of Lords would become law. hitherto, the land hod been too much in the hands of a few, Cal it svas Onto that the people es a whole bed more power over it. (Applause). Mr. Et it, mid be hoped the splendid series of open. air meetings would end in Warrineton being true to itself, and that at the first possible occasion the people would put therimelvee right once egain end mad as the repreteutati is of Warrington in the House of Commons • member of the dernocrsiic and progressive party in the person of their esteemed end popular townsman, Mr. A. 11. Crosfleld. (Applause.) We were living in stirring times for Liberalism. The Lords had at lent been brought to MT, and they did not like it. Laughter.) The maultict of tbe Opposition in the House of Commons that day hod bordered on the linen of bleckguerdiem, and woe as outrage on the decencies of Parliamentary delate. Epithets like " Traitor " and " Ciptain Ford " were burled by members of the so-c kited gentlemsnly party at • Prime Minister who, iii the ostimatiou of Liberals, Wm one of the bravest and boldest who bad ever sit in the House of Common•—(aopleuse)—• Prime kl ulster whose risme would be Ivinde.l lows to posterity as one of the greitest and ablest of those great Liber..l Prime alinieters who bad held the destinies of this country he their bend, Mr. Asquith, by his tenacity and restrsint, by his parseverance and moderation, not less than by his courage and tact, had secured for [be people one of the greatest triumphs sines the Reform Act of 1832. (Applaum.) July 21st, 1211, would pass into the peges of England's history as a day worthy to 1,3 reckoned with May 17th, 1'132. THE EXAMINER.
SATURDAY, JULY 29 1911.
There is, of course, no THE MOROCCAN ground for the repre- CRISIS. sentation that the KING

has abandoned his !intention of spending the week at Goodwood because of what our Tory contemporaries continue to call the Constitutional crisis. It may have been necessary for His MAJESTY to spend Monday in London in connection with the procedure on the Parliament Bill. But there was no reason for breaking further than that into a contemplated week of pleasure, which must have been all the more grateful because it came after prolonged, if agreeable, toil. What has kept HIS MAJESTY in London is obviously the Morocco situation. The Parliamentary crisis is no longer acute. AU the necessary arrangements have been made. On the other hand, the Morocco crisis may last for some months to come. It is at present the occasion of many communications, and, it must be admitted, of some uneasiness. The complication is one that would grow more serious the more it was treated by this country as if it were only a remote concern. The Government has been quick,however, to note that British interests were in danger, alike in the neighbourhood of Gibraltar and the region of the Congo. It has taken action which gives us the keenest possible concern. In the 'conversations" that are taking place between France and Germany, some- thing may happen within a day or even an 'hour that may be of the greatest importance. This is why the KING remains in town. What Mr. LI OYD GEORGE said on Friday last, and what is now taking place at the Foreign Office and the Admiralty, has, as might have been expected, stirred the blood of the ordinary jingo. He has, after his habit, begun to clamour for war with Germany. His maxim and guiding principle is, "Better fight Germany now than a few years hence, when she will be stronger." This is the policy of Donnybrook Fair, as described by Thackeray "Tim, there's a bald hid show- ing under the canvas of the tint. Faith, I must land it one." It is surely unnecessary to say that such a policy as this has no place -among the designs of a Liberal Government. By nations in their senses wars are not made in order to prevent wars that might occur in some unknown future. The strong nation is one that places itself in so invulnerable a position that it can not only avoid war, but operate as a strong influence in favour of peace. The purpose of fleets and armies is to fight, no doubt,in the ultimate resort. But their primary use is to give convincing force to reasons that may be advanced against fighting. "Oh! "says the jingo; "here is LLOYD-GEORGE talking like one of us." Nothing of the kind. The CHANCELLOR OF THE EXCHEQUER talked like a statesman who knows that for us the price of peace like that of liberty is eternal vigilance. Mr. LLOYD GEORGE'S speech at the Mansion House changed much, as it was expected to do. It at once made it clear to other Powers concerned that when negotia- tions about territory are taking place British interests in that part of the world which is concerned must not be treated as if they did not exist. In consequence, some exaspera- tion has been caused in one quarter at least, and, perhaps, some surprise also. The Act of Algeciras was being torn up as if it concerned nobody but France and Germany. That is not ths case. That is why Mr. sourrir announced that new seriousness had been given to the situation. A large part of Africa cannot be passed over as a pawn in a game, were there any disposition to pass it over,without rous- ing the keen interest of Downing-street. This being so, it becomes necessary OM the truth should be stated with all due emphasis. The statements of loth Ministers must necessarily have a moderating influence on such negotiations as are taking place. It is such firm treatment as must undoubtedly make for peace where there does not exist a determination for war at any price. It is our clear opinion that no such I determination exists anywhere, and that the Morocco crisis will come to a quite peaceful and satisfactory end, though not, it is probable, for some weeks or some months to come.
Probably, sheer love THE CASE OF of the limelight, and REBELLIOUS the fact that brother

HAROLD! "FE." was manipulat- ing the lantern, had a lot to do with Mr. Harold Smith, M.P., -throwing in his lot with the rebels who espoused the "No surrender" policy on the Veto, cast aside as invertebrate and worthless the leadership of Lord Lansdowne and Mr. Balfour, and howled down the Prime Minister in his own House. By now he has had time to reflect, and may possibly be wondering how the loyal Tories of Warrington view his excursion into political buccaneering. What the Liberals and non-party electors think, he will doubtless be able accurately to surmise. Warringtcn has been accustomed to be represented by members who attached a high value to the decencies and courtesies of political life, and who placed loyalty to their party chiefs second only to their fidelity to the constituency which returned them. Now, the position is changed. The snatch-election of December last placed the representation of War- xicgton in the hands of a young man

whose political balance seems decidedly unreliable and who may follow any will-o'-th'-wisp, which for the moment glitters like a guiding star across the political bog-land. In one short week, the Tory hot-bloods have disgraced their party and failed ignominously in their aims and objects. To-day they are the objects of scorn and derision on all sides, and it would be fitting and proper for any Warrington elector— preferably an honest Tory—to take the first opportunity of publicly asking the Member for Warrington what explanation he has to offer for his association with the discredited " Hughligans " of Westminster.

Education has been SCHOOLS, NEW much to the fore in AND OLD. Warrington this week. The spirited way in which the Education Committee has addressed itself to the task of providing adequate and up-to-date school accommoda- tion found further exemplification on Wednesday when the Mayor laid the founda- tion stone of the Evelyn-street Council School—the third building of its kind which the ratepayers have been called upon to provide since the 1902 Act came into force. Great progress has already been made with the erection of the school which promises to be a model of its kind. Even if the external ornamentation does not happen to be as lavish as Alderman , Bennett would desire, the arrangements of the various departments are most happily planned. We are glad to see that children who show a preference for craftsmanship will have every opportunity of developing their skill in the manual training depart- ment. In one important respect Evelyn- street school has the honour of leading the way, for we hear it is the first elementary school in the country to be fitted with don( he baths. It is expected that a swimming bath will follow when the Local Government Board can be prevailed upon to sanction a loan for that purpose. The Mayor's speech at the ceremony on Wednesday raised ' seve:al points of exceptional interest, and there will be a general endorsement of his Worship's view that as the Education Committee is, quite properly, devoting much attention to physically and mentally defec- tive children it should also put forth special efforts to enable abnormal ability, or genius, to make the best of itself in the race of life. To turn from the new to th 3 old, the annual Speech Day, in connection with the Boteler Grammar School on Thursday, gave striking evidence —if any were needed—of the wonderful vitality and usefulness of an institu- tion which boasts long and worthy traditions. Archdeacon Cunningham's speech struck out on original lines and its homeliness and practicality commended it to every section of the audience. In these days of lofty orations on the abstract topic of education, it is refreshing to hear a few direct and pointed words on the importance of good manners and a warning against the priggishness which success is sometimes apt to induce.

We hear from London NUMBER 13. of an amusing comedy concerning the number 13. A lady who lets apartments found that with this number her house did not attract people as she had reason to expect it would, and after a long run of bad luck she decided to convert the unlucky number into 12A. This was done, and we may assume that immedi- ately afterwards her house was profitably filled. But presently a hard-headed Borough Council discovered what had happened, and sternly refused to recognise the change. But the busy landlady cared nothing for Borough Councils and" sich like things," and 12A re- mained upon her door. Meanwhile,the Council has been consulting the London County Council, and between them they have I decided that the proper numerical sequence must be restored at all costs, and they have given the Borough Surveyor powers to enforce their decision. So probably in a day or two we hear of a long-drawn tussle—with a paint brush—between the resolute land- lady and the unhappy surveyor. We hope the landlady will win, for though the super- stition is utterly illogical and absurd it is, at any rate,an unlucky number for her. She has to think of her livelihood, and if people will not live in a house numbered 13 she must do something to appease them. It is strange that superstition should have clung so persistently , to the number, for in some parts of the world I it is actually honoured. In the Indian Pantheon are thirteen Buddhas; both Indian and Chinese pagodas are surrounded with thirteen mystical discs. Japan also has many sacred associations with the number. When the American States were first united there were thirteen of them; its motto had and has thirteen letters, and its eagle has thirteen feathers. Ancient Mexico venerated the number, and had thirteen gods and thirteen days to its week, and many other similar associations with the number in other parts of the world can be mentioned. Yet we cherish the idea that it is unlucky, and not only can we give no plausible reason for the superstition ; we cannot even discover how it originated.

It will be good news LAND TRANSFER to thousands of owners
REFORM.
of lend . property.. that

the Lord .-Chrancellor is at last preparing a bill on the basis of the recommendations of the Royal Commission on the Land Transfer Acts. That Commission was appointed at the request of the Incor- porated Law Society, and, to the considerable surprise of the legal profession,it did not con- deirn but approved of the principle of regis- tration of title. In a fine speech in the House of Lords, which we strongly recommend every landowner to read, the Lord Chan- cellor said that " the present condition of the law in England as regards the title to landed property and the methods of trans- ferring it amounts to a scandal, and is almost unique for its obscurity and costliness." As everyone who has sold or bought land knows to his sorrow, all deeds and documents relating to it for years past have to be produced and examined at each sale, and even then there is no security that the title is good. The position is altogether ridiculous, and it is amazing that it has continued so long. Contrary to the general impression there are a large number of solicitors who would welcome a remedy in the form of a Government register and guarantee of title. If it would mean smaller fees for them, it would also mean that land would be a much more "liquid" security, and that, consequently, they would have many more transactions to negotiate. Land- owners have nothing to lose and everything to gain by such a remedy, and it is surpris- ing that long ago they did not join hands and press for the reform of the present but obso- lete law. In no sense whatever is it a party question, and there is a guarantee of this in the fact that there are no keener advocates of reform than Lord Halsbury, the last Con- servative Lord Chancellor,and Lord Loreburn, the present Liberal Lord Chancellor.

THE NEW LIBERAL LECTURE VAN. There will be a great rally of Liberals at Bridge Foot this (Saturday) evening when the opening of the new Liberal lecture van will be celebrated by the holding of a mass meeting at seven o'clock. Mr. C. E. Parker will preside and the principal speakers will be Mr. A. H. Crosfield, Mr. Fred Maddison, and Mr. Harry New. The van, which is to be opened at the beginning of the meeting by Mr. A. H. Crosfield, will greatly facilitate the propaganda work which is to be vigorously carried on in the town. When Mr. Harry New came to Warrington he at once realized the necessity tor a van in order that open-air meetings might be held in every part of the constituency. With characteristic energy he applied himself to the task of collecting subscriptions and the appeal met with such a generous response that a thoroughly up-to-date and well-appointed van has been purchased. The lorry has been built by Mr. J. Knight, London Bridge, Stockton Heath, and the van itself by Mr. G. Wallington, of Froghall-lane, Warrington. The painting is the work of Messrs. W. Winstanley and Son, Park Place, Warrington, the lettering having been executed by Mr. R. H. Pooley. Prominently displayed on the exterior of the van are the words " Warrington Liberal Association Van" and "Liberalism means government by the people." One side of the van is so constructed that the lower part will open out and form a railed platform, projecting three feet and supported by posts. There is seating accommodation for about fifteen persons and the van is furnished with book shelves, pictures, arc. It is the intention of the Liberal Association to hold a lantern lecture campaign during the autumn and winter months, when the important topics of the day will he expounded. She van will also be placed at the disposal of the League of Young Liberals, the Progressive Labour League, and the Women's Liberal Association.

The Committee has I considered the questior. and decided that it be deferred—until winter presumably. • We are glad to note that the Corporation is taking advantage of the County Council's application for a loan for the widening of Sankey Bridges to lodge an objection either with the Local Government Board or at the I local inquiry. We are reminded (says the "Westminster Gazette ") of the man who starts out in a fog, and, after walking about all day, finds himself at the end of the journey on his own doorstep. What a lot of trouble would have been saved if the " Times" had only stuck all through to the admission it made B,t the time of the General Election. 0 A woman's "editorial association " had a dinner in Topeka recently, and one of the toasts ran: " Woman ! without her, man is a brute." But the compositor, cynical and married no doubt, set this up as : "Woman, without her man, is a brute." The story reminds the " Elinburgh Evening Dispatch of the way in which the old Wick precentor read out a certain intimation for prayer which had been banded to him. The intima- tion ran : "Captain So-and-So having gone to sea, his wife desires the prayers of the congregation." But the bold, bad precentor put the comma after "wife," and so read :1 "Captain So-and-So, having gone to see his wife, desires the prayers of the congregation."

Sir William Willcicks, who is coming home through ill-health, from Mesopotamia, where he has superintended such extensive irrigation works, once expressed the opinion that the precise spot of the situ- ation of the garden of Eden is in the Hairlah district, 250 kilometres north of Bagdad. The spot is a verdant oasis, situated in the centre of a vast desolate plain, traversed by four arms of the Euphrates, representing, Sir William Willcocks suggests, the four rivers of the Garden of Eden. As to the deluge, Sir William's notion is that the dams or dykes built by the pastoral dwellers to con- serve the waters of the Euphrates and the Tigris burst, and that the plain between the Irivers was submerged and that the greater part of the population were drowned. Noah, he suggests, knowing the condition of the dams and foreseeing their collapse built the ark and escaped the inundation. It is quite an irrigation expert's theory, though one which may or may not find favour with the theologians.

• • We had the novel experience on Tuesday morning, just before 8 o'clock, of being awakened by an aeroplane. Of course, we are aware that we ought to have been out in the garden hours before catching the early worm, but the fact remains that we were asleep when Mr. Melly's monoplane throbbed through the still morning air at Grappen- hall, and passed over our humble roof at a low altitude but a high speed, For a moment we thought the fire engine was at work near by, and then as consciousness fully dawned, we leapt to the window and caught sight of the daring aviator flying directly into the eye of the sun. Other people also saw him, and still others heard the sound of his flight and heeded not—to their great disappointment later. Mr. Melly.was in Manchester a quarter of an hour after passing over Grappeohall,l and one felt a sympathetic interest in learn- ing from the evening papers that he had smashed that sleep-dispelling monoplane while experimenting in the afternoon. The return journey of the machine was less thrilling, for, like a crippled warrior, it was borne through the highways and streets recumbent on a motor-lurry.

div.head: WARRINGTON CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.
div.p: WARRINGTON CHILDREN'S SUMMER CAMP.

One hundred and twenty-one girls set off from the Prdl Hall last Saturday morning for the camp at Preslatyn. They were accompanied by nix ladies who have taken care of them during the week namely : liebbington, Davenport, Ellison, Poser, Niande Ems. and Mrs. Burge. On arriving at Preniatyn the children were placed in processional order and marched to camp ahem they were pl.ed in elections for the various huts. An excellent meal was served and was greatly enjoyed. After dinner the children played games in the field ; they then had tea and atterward• prepared their herb s for the night. On Sunday the children were early astir and after the Usual morning work the Roman C Allelic girls were taken to church at Prestatyn, the Church of England section joining the children of Meliden in a special service in the afternoon. The evening was spent on the shore. . . .

On Monday morning the children walked along the shore to see the pierrots, whose songs and jokes were greatly enjoyed. The afttruoto and evening were -spent on the shore. On Tuesday the girls were taken to view the beauti- ful Waterfall at Dyserth, the return journey being made through the woods on the mountain side. All arrived home quite safely. On Wednesday morning the flierrota were again visited, the afternoon being spent on the Camp ground and shore. On Thursday the children went foes ramble through the nut groves on the mountain side, returning via Meliden.
• Friday was a very busy day. The children quieted in preparing the huts for the second batch of girls who will strive to-may. The health of the girls generally has been very prod.

div.head: Wesley Guild Garden Party.
div.p: Wesley Guild Garden Party.

The Weerley Childs of the Warrington district held a joint garden party in the beautiful grounds of the National Children's Horne and Orphanage Frodsham, on Saturday. The majority of the 200 Guilders travelled by train, the rest proceeding by cycle. la the after- noon sportn were indulged io, and in this connection the ladies were not forgotten, as is no often the case. 'ren was served in toe large schoolroom, the serving gis ng general satisfaction. An inspection was made , of the several large buildings, in which over a hundred !children arc housed, and the pleasant aurroundings of there previously friemiless children were cause for eulogistic comment. The party travelled home by the 040 train—We may mention that this week-end the various Guilds are making a strret and house to hone° collection, whereby it is hopol to raise a substaxtisl amount to help onthe homes or the Natienal Children's Ilome and Orphanage Society, of which the Frodsham institution in only one of several. would especially ascend to heaven that Mrs. Watson might be tustained sod comforted in her great sorrow. Mr. Watson was not a man who sought for personal prominence, or who cared for the language of eulogy, and he would deprecate any extended reference of that kind. Fut he was a valuable and rueful, and willing and kindly men, whose death was a very !teflona loss to their commtmity. Ile was not in membership with that, church, retaining to the end his connection with the Preabyterian body. hut he probably would have remained with them, at least en fellow worshipper and willing helper, had his life been prolonged. They regarded his death with most eincere regretond trusted that his memory would not easily pass from their grateful and respectful recollection.

div.head: St. John's Presbyterian Church.
div.p: St. John's Presbyterian Church.

At St. John's on Roeder evening last the Fee. W Reid preached on "Old Testament Communion with God," taking for his text the story of Enoch, who " walked with God," as related in Genesis v.21-lb. Mr. Reid slid Enoch stood for " communion with God," and, calling attention to (ho words of verse 2:1," Enoch walked with God after he begat Methuselah," mid he Was rum there were great numbers of Scripture readers who had never noticed this—that Enoch walked with CLid after the birth of his flrat child. Probably he had hod his face set towards the light from his earliest days but there came something into his life with the advent of hie first born that bound him nearer to the aide of his Lord and Mmter th,n ever he had been before. There wore periods in the lives of men and women which were ningulerly propitiom for the walking closely with God, and if there were one seison more than another it Wan when a man and woman came together, and became one after God's holy ordinance and when the home became altered by the advent into It of a little life. If there was a time to walk with God that was the time. They did not necemarily walk ' with God tthen they turned their faces towarda His house, when they read his word, song Ilii praises or bowed the head in prayer. It Wan something more than that. When the spirit surrendered iteelf to Him completely, and became meek. even as Christ was meek, when they became more Godlike by being morn Christ- like—when they were seeking God in thet spirit then they were walking with God. Enoch had nom of the advantages they possessed to-day, and he witnessed for God in the midst of untoward circimatanom. They couldnot awe to-day that it was n difficult thing to witness for God and to walk with Him.

A GOSSIP ABOUI THE SWEET PEA. They say that the Queen's favourite flower is the sweet pea. If this be so, then many of us are in the fashion, for we too pre-1 fee the sweet pea above everything else. Is there, or could there be, anything sweeter in fragrance or with such rich diversity of colpurir g . . . . .

-1-arin—ioing to gossip just a little about the sweet pea. The flower that is best known to us is of course a cultivated one but there are many native peas among our wild flowers which get along very nicely without the aid of a gardener. The best known of 'our native peas is the Meadow Vetchling, a pretty plant with yellow flowers that may be found in the hedges all over the country. The structure of the wild Meadow Vetchling is exactly similar to that of the sweet pea. The petals are made up of five distinct parts; the uppermost of the five is much larger than the others and is called the standard. Then there are two side petals known as wings, and lastly, two that go to make what is called the keel, because they have something of a boat-shape about them. Every sweet pea then has a standard, two wings and the keel (made up of two parts of the petal joined together). If you examine the keel when it is ripe you will find that it is just what we call the pod of the pea with seeds or peas along its edges. The sweet pea is just another of "God's thoughts of beauty taking form to gladden mortal gaze." The old monks who gave names to most of our wild plants were very fanciful in their remarks about the order of plants to which the sweet pea belongs, and made quite a little parable out of the flower. To them the standard pointing upward stood for a disciple raising the hand as a pledge of loyalty to God. The two wings suggested to them the human soul in the attitude of flight, and the keel was to them symbolic of readiness to cross the sea with the seed of the Kingdom to deposit in the hearts of the receptive souls. This may be fanciful, but it is very beautiful and very suggestive.

div.head: PILGRIMAGES ROUND ABOUT WILMSLOW , AND SOME WAYSIDE GOSSIP.
div.p: PILGRIMAGES ROUND ABOUT WILMSLOW , AND SOME WAYSIDE GOSSIP.

The pilgrim can seldom go wrong in Cheshire. All that is needed is an historic imagination and a little patience to carry out a task of research. Given these two things the old dead homesteads live again, and quiet lanes bustle with movement.

The present journey is a short run through lanes that promise little of interest. We are going to Wilmslow and disembark with cycle and map at Altrincham, thence to pick our quiet path through Ringway to Morley.

AMWAY'S HERO. It is not every tiny village that can boast a hero, but Ringway has got an uncommon one, and we will begin with the story. Once upon a day the Duke of Cumberland passed through Ringway with his fighting force. He was pursuing the retreating High- landers, and was hard upon their heels. Among the village crowd that stood to gaze upon the soldiers was a young man of twenty-four named Isaac Podmore. Six and a half feet in height he stood high above his fellows, and as the Duke passed he pulled up to look more carefully at the owner of the head shoulders that rose so conspicuously above the rest. Without the ceremony of an introduc- _ . _ . .
ion the Duke called out to' Isaac to fall in
the ranks. The raw youth did so without a moment for thought. The fact that his legs and arms came a woeful distance

through the biggest uniform was a detail that did not affect his pride, and was easily put right by the ordering of a special outfit. Away to Scotland he went unzained and unused to war as he was,and there fought on the famous field of Culloden. Following the defeated Highlanders into their own north country he tried to settle down there. He married a Highland lass and set up home,but the experiment as far as home-making was concerned was not a great success. He did not leave the army and when a war summons came he was ready again for the fray. For forty years he was in the army and saw many a hard fight. In Flanders he was badly wounded in the leg but refused to believe he was hurt and went on fighting. The only thing t 1 at temporary quietened him was a bullet which struck him full in the mouth. Fortunately the mouth was open and was sufficiently large to give a bullet play. The lead passed out at the back of the neck and Isaac had at last to admit that he was hurt.

But it was only a trifling interruption in a great career. After forty years of following the flag he sought out his native village and demonstrated that he was as safe off the field as upcn. it by living until he was ninety. . . .
The fate Of the Highland lassie we have not been able to discover. It is a pity, for she could hardly have been lacking in courage. _ MORLEY AND ITS PASSIVE RESISTERS. _ . .

Morley too has nurtured heroes; lots of them. It was an early Quaker centre and the disciples of George Fox became quite numerous in the very first days of the society. As early as 1653 there was a meet- ing here and the pilgrim who likes to study things that are really historic must bestow a glance upon their old chapel. It stands on the edge of the Moss and is now converted into cottages. There is a graveyard also, sheltered by a clump of trees, and the sun lights up the tiny decaying stones as we nag.T. . . _

Here rest some of the early heroes of religious freedom. Quiet sufferers in life they rest quietly here in death, quite content, no doubt, with the stand they took and greatly content that the world has confirmed their judgment. Of one of those who rests here a story is preserved that deserves a place in the annals of passive resistance. The quaker had refused the Church tithe and the authorities proceeded to distrain upon his goods. He kept bees, and as a means of making themselves obnoxious claimed one of the swarms. Taking the hive they proceeded to annoy him by shaking the insects loose in the house and then prepared to carry off the hive. "Nay, friend," said the quaker very quietly, "Thee has claimed the bees not the hive. The bees are thine, but the hive is mine; take thy bees but just leave thee the hive where thou found it."
LYCH GATE AND TOWER WILMSLOW PARISH CHURCH,

div.head: WILMSLOW CHURCH.
div.p: WILMSLOW CHURCH.
We pass from the quaker graveyard to the home of their persecutors, these latter sleeping as quietly under stone as the quakers under the peaty sod.

The Church has a rare old parish chest cut from a solid block of oak made to "keepe the register bookes in." The " bookes " that rest there have some curious entries (we read this from a penny guide book as we sit in church) one of them being Given to John Downes a free gift for killing several urchins, 4d.

This is very dreadful on first reading and raises visions of irate motorists (or cyclists) bribing the said John Downes to rid the roads of two-legged creatures that will get in the way. But we remember that we are now "back in history" and that an urchin is really a four-legged prickly thing. The same book records that twopence was allowed to the churchwardens for powder and shot to rid the church of pigeons that were building there.

We -nearly milord the best thing in Wilmslow Church. Thanks to a little maid we were shown, snugly protected by the matting a beautiful fifteenth-century incised brass that marks the grave of Sir Robert le Botha and Douce his wife. Sir Robert is

living in a particular place. The Govern- ment has also accepted this principle in fixing the wages, or salaries I should say, of its Civil Servants.

Both in this country ard in the colonies the principle of a minimum wage has been embodied in legislation. In this country we have the Trades Boards, which have the legal power to fix a minimum wage for certain scheduled trades. It is not a 308. minimum,it is true, that these Trades Boards are able to fix, hut there the principle is accepted and applied. lithe I.L.P. could continue its agitation for a legal 30s. minimum until it had made so much public opinion that Parliament was obliged to give attention to the matter, it is pretty certain that whatever Parliament did it would not attempt to carry out the I.L.P. demand in full. I do not think the I.L.P. expects that it will succeed in getting the universal minimum of 30s. just yet. But it is always well to aim higher than one expects to reach.

ANOTHER CHILD-MARRIAGE STORY. Singularly enough we are to encounter another story of child-marriage the same afternoon. As we cycle away from Wilmslow to make our way to Cheadle Station we pass Handforth and turn aside to see Handforth Hall. This is one of Cheshire's fine old buildings, and though spoiled by a brick easing the place is very old. William Honford, who lived here, perished on Flodden field. With him on that great day was his young son-in-law, Sir John Stanley. Possibly Sir John had been married to the lady to secure theproperty.At any rate after Flodden be entered into postlession of Handforth Hall with his twelve-year-old wife.

Not long after, Sir John became embroiled in a quarrel about some titles, and Cardinal Wolsey who heard the case seems to have sent him to prison. The strain upon his nerves was too much. He became "embittered against earthly matters" and decided to ask for a divorce that he might enter a monastery. His wife was quite willing and agreed to enter a nunnery.So they signed an agreement by which they bound themselves "to relinquish all and singular the pomps, vanities, pleasures, and delecta- tions of this world." Sir John became a monk and took up his abode at Westminster where he engraved his adopted motto "Allis Vanity." Lady Margaret evidently gave herself time to think before taking refuge in a nunnery, and decided to give things one more trial before deciding that all was vanity. She married Sir Usiah Brereton and proceeded to make things comfortable at Handforth Hall. As we look up at the doorway we decipher her initials carved with his and can easily make out the Brereton crest and the date 1562.
Let us hope that Lady Margaret's experiment with the " pomps, vanities and delectations" was a complete success. A.M.

div.head: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
div.p: FROM LABOUR'S STANDPOINT.
By Philip Snowden, NP,
THIRTY SHILLINGS A WEEK ALL
ROUND.

The Independent Labour Party is carrying on during this summer a very vigorously conducted campaign in favour of a Thirty Shillings a Week Minimum Wage and a Universal Eight Hours Day. The rank and file of the party have taken up this agitation with very great vigour, and successful meetings are being held all over the country. I doubt whether the results of such an agita- tion are likely to be very permanent. If I remember rightly the Party had a similar campaign last year for a month or so in favour of the Minority Report proposals for the Break up of the Poor Law. Unless such a crusade be sustained, it is more than likely that the effect is only temporary, and that after a very short time the usefulness of the agitation has disappeared. Of the two proposals which are now engaging the attention of the 1.L.P., I think the latter one mentioned, namely, a Shorter Working Day, is the more important. This is a question which is within the regions of practicability and probability. It with widely advocated twenty years ago, and in the meantime, though little has been heard of it except in respect of the coal trade, the Eight Hours Day has been secured in a good many trades by arrangement between the masters and the men. The responsible leaders of such great trade unions as those connected with the cotton trade and the printing trade have committed themselves to a demand for an eight hours day, or a forty- eight hours week. So that the I.L.P.'s demand for a general legal Eight Hours Day is a practical and possible proposal, and a sustained agitation by them for this reform, backed up by the . help of the organised trades, should have a . substantial result. In two of the great busi- nesses of the country, namely, the textile • trade and the railway service, the time and the industry are ripe for such a reform. But ' in regard to the other item in the I.L.P.'s present agitation, one cannot speak in quite the same strain. The I.L.P, itself, I presume, does not put forward the demand for a universal minimum wage of 30s. a week as a proposal which can be carried out immedi- ately. The demand is put forward as a means of drawing attention to the lowness of the wages of a great proportion of the workers, and of the need and the justice of every adult worker having a wage which • will enable him to live a civilised and human ; life.

div.head: PIONEER WORK
div.p: A PIONEER WORK

From that point of view the agitation is good. It is the business of pioneers to be always far ahead of the general body. Such a body as the I.L.P. must preach the ideal. It must fire the people's imagination and make them determined •to have some improvement. It is its business to make the people discontent with poverty and ignor- ance. When it has done that the" practical statesman" comes along, and begins to trans- late the ideal into a definite proposal for legislation. He is always a cautious man,and his proposal never is open to the criticism that he is going too far for a beginning. The I.L.P. is not for the first time putting forward the idea of a minimum wage. That principle has been recognised in various ways already both in practice and in legisla- tion. The Post Office acts on that idea in fixing the wages of the postal employees. Their wages are regulated by the cost of

div.head: VI COCOA has won the VICTORY
div.p: VI COCOA has won the VICTORY
SOME USEFUL ROSULTS.

If we can get the idea of a minimum wage into the heads of the people we shall have done an extremely useful work. We shall have got the people to look to themselves as the State, and to understand the power they have as Ibrganized citizens to better their conditions. We shall have got the people to recognise that the community has an obliga- tion upon it to see that none of its workers are doing useful labour at a remuneration which does not allow a human existence. We shall have got rid of the idea that the workman must be the last of the co-partners in production to be considered, and that if the industry will not "pay more" he must be content with starvation wages. When Parliament does undertake to enforce a universal Minimum Wage it is not likely that it will be 30s. a week all round for a start. But if we can get a beginning with something less, then a real advance has been made.

If the I.L.P. proposal were to be regarded as one which is put forward for immediate adoption without any exceptions or modifica- tions,then it could be shattered into molecules by the force of hard facts hurled against it. To carry out such a proposal as that, except by gradual steps which will allow the industries affected to adapt themselves to the ehanges,would mean absolute ruin to the industries of the country. Take agriculture, for instance. The official figures as to the wages of agricultural labourers put their earnings, I think, much too high. But even these figures show that the wage is below a pound a week. There must be, I should say, half a million labourers whose wages are below 15s. a week. I am putting it very moderately. To raise the wages of these to not less than 30s. a week would cost about £20,000,000 a year, which is five times more than the total paid by farmers in income tax, according to the income tax returns. Take another illustration, that of domestic service. There are over two million women employed in this work for wages. There is not one in a thousand of them who will now be earning a wage of 30s. a week. Suppose that by law their employers were required to ruse the wages of each domestic servant to not less than 30s. a week. It would cost at least £60,000,000 a year. The immediate effect of this would be that two-thirds of them would be dismissed at the end of the first month. The same thing would be happening in every other trade, and we should have two-thirds of the workers turned out of employment, and the whole of the industry of the country would be brought to a state of chaos.

Thirty shillings a week is sadly littlo enough for an adult worker. By well- thought-out reforms I believe it is possible to ensure that and more. But it cannot be done by simply passing a law that every- body shall have not less than 30s. a week regardless offsets. So long as the land and instruments of produaion are in the hands of the private owners it will always be difficult to get any reform which will be more than a slight palkative. The thing, it seems to me, which it would be best for the I.L.P. to concentrate upon would be the nationalisation of the land and the mines and the railways. Then there would be little difficulty, after these were national property, in getting the minimum wage. It would be given to all railway men and to all miners without any dislocation of trade. Then other trades could be nationalised, and the standard for the workers raised. Since the municipalisation of the tramways in so many towns there has been a considerable raising of the minimum wage, and on the average, I should say it is not far off the ideal 30s. a week now.
The LL P. is doing good " propaganda work" by its agitation for a 308. minimum. It will make the people think, and thinking is a necessary preliminary to action.

div.p: CH A PTER VI.

Robert Ilennhall was buried. Ile was fol- lowed to bin grave by a great number of friends, for there wee no one who did not respect the kind and excellent man. All sort. of proffer, of sympathy were given to Rebecca. Her particular friends, the Lorri, mere, were most slalom, that she should leave the gloomy house and come to them, but the girl refused to stir. She wits not in the mood to flee anyone. She was, in short, abnolutely broken down. Her love for her father had been strong, tenacious, no deep, so firm, so constant, that no other great lore had hitherto touched her.

Rebecca was twenty years of age, but had never loved anyone as she loved her father. Now he was dead, and it !seemed to her that all the world had stopped. Mho followed him to hi. last resting place in her deep black, and more than one person turned to look at the pale, noble face, and more than one person also observed Mary Gray an she walked behind Rebecca, and stood almost by her side an the girl bent over the open grave. . . • '•• •

When the funeral was at an end the will was read, leaving everything that Henshall possessed to his daughter. The money was tied up, and in the hands of trustees, until Rebecca came of age. For a year, therefore, she was not completely her own mistress, but very ample provisions had been made foi her, and she might demand any sum of money she required within reason. Rebecca's requirements were simple. She would like to stay on in the old house: she did not want company. Her servants were faithf.ul;.silie would, by degrees, see her
friends. Her great desire wasuto continue the old life. Her lawyer, Mr. Flower, expostu- lated with the girl. •• • • • •
"You are young, and, pardon me, attrac- tive," he said. "You will soon change your mind."

She looked at him with her beautiful eyes, and her sad mouth looked sadder than ever. He saw that there was little use in urging any course of action upon her just at present, and prepared to go sway, telling her to apply to him if she wse in any need. As he was leaving the room, however, she called him back.

"I was forgetting," she maid, "there in something which I nhould like at once. I want you to put to my credit in the bank, in my own name, about one thourand pounds." "It Allan be done, Minn Henshall." . . . _
"I have a small 'account in the City of London Bank already, but I want this par. ticular _sum. How soon can I have it?"

The lawyer looked at liii7wate-n-..- "I will see that the money is forthcoming, and entered to your credit before the bank closes this afternoon," he said. "Thank you," said Rebecca. "I. there anything else?" asked Mr. Flower.
" No, not to day ; thank you very much in deed.

_ She shook hands with him. She was quite brave and calm. She had shed no tears during the whole of that trying day. As soon an Flower had gone Rebecca rang the study bell sharply. Lucy appeared. "Lucy, can you tell me where Miss Gray is?"
I don't know, miss; perhaps she is in her

"Find her if you can, and tell her that I shall be glad to speak to her at once." "Yes, miss." When Lucy departed, Rebecca went to a small desk, which was her own special possession, and where her father loved her to sit when she wrote her girlish letters. She unlocked the desk, and took her cheque book out. 'the quickly filled in is cheque for • certain slim, rebuked the desk, •nd was standing by the fire with the open cheque in her hand when Mary Gray appeared. "You have sent for me?" said Mary. "Yes, I have sent for you. Will you shut the door, please. I have just a feet words to Mary came forward. She was wearing black, and her fri,ckled, pale face looked paler then ever, her very light blue eyes lighter, and her hair more devoid of colour. Beside Rebecca, whose eyes were no dark sad of et, intense a blue, and whore hair was block as • raven's wing, she seemed alto- gether • creature destitute of either beauty or character. But Rebecca's mouth, firm as it was, beautifully curved as it was, and pathetic as was its expression, was not as firm as those tightly closed lips of Mary's, nor wan her manner more assured than that of the girl who was only—as she was proud or saying—s poor dependent. "I don't want to hurt you,'' said Rebecca. You have been with on for some time." "Five years exactly," said Mary. "Yes," .

"And during that time, said Mary, "I have, I think, done my utmost to pleaw you and my dear late employer, Mr. Bettinall." Rebecca bowed. She could not bear to hear her father's name mentioned. After • minute's pause, she said : "My father and I had • little conversation about you during the last few minute. of hie life."

---"WeI! do I know that," thought Mary; but ahe una outwardly talent. "In obedience to his wishes, I have sent for you now," continued Rebecca. "I am Norry if I most say something to pain you. You are engaged to Mr. Arnold Deep," "That in no news," said Mary. "Why should it be mentioned now r . . .
. • "My father dad not approve of 0245 engage- ment. '

"He told me no," said Mary ; "but it was my concern, not his; and I do not see that he had a right to.interfere. I am of age; I am twenty-five years old." Well, Mary," said Rebecca, "I will not prolong thin interview, but according to my father's instructions, I hare it in my power to offer you two thousand pounds, on the sole condition that you do iud marry Mr. Arnold Deepe. My father did not think well of him, nor do I. The money will have to be tied op securely, and for • certain time—only the in. Wrest allowed to vou. This interest will be instantly stopped if you marry Mr. Metre; but, on the other hand, if a fitting opportu- gity comes, and it is really known that you
have completely broken with him, I shall be willing to hand you the whole capital to start you in any way of business you prefer. But that, of course, cannot be done for some time.''

you," said Mary. "Your father was good enough to make me a similar offer. Ile made it on that night when you were en- joying yonritelf at the dance at the Town Hall, and before you were kind enough to I"-'d ma. tr hi. ic o night, I mined hint. He owed all his cont. forte and all the attentiona he received, to me. I may as well tell you frankly that I had very nearly made up my mind to accept hie offer and to break with poor Arnold. But when you returned in the morning, you used intemperate words to me, and, to be frank with you, I—l hated you I hate you still, itebeees•lienshall; and I wil'A not give op in, lover for your sake." "Very well, Mary; I urn not going to urge it. It was my duty to tell you what my father said. I have now fulfilled that duty, and the matter can close. But I have something else to add. My father particularly wished the connection between us to he severed. Ilia wishes are sacred to me, and as you "

frankly nay you hate me, •I may an lion frankly reply on my part that I have no love for you, that in no one partiettler do you suit me. I shall be glad, therefore, if you will make arrangements to leave this house, and I am prepared to give you two hundred pound• if you will do no this afternoon. have • cheque in my hand drawn in your favour for that amount. You can take it to my honk to morrow morning, and it will be honoured."

"Two hundred pounds!" said Mary. She gasped a little; she put her hand on the back of her chair and her hand trembled. She was a daring and wicked woman, but she had newer in the whole of her existence owned any som approaching this. Arnold'. talk of the thousands which would be his, seemed to Mary like the dreams of a mad- man; but this two hundred pounds wag tan- gible, and almost within her grasp. "Bat,' idle said, with • little shiver— "wino I go today? . .
"Yes —l't once,'please; as soon as you can pack your things.' "1 here been with you five years, and you treat me no !" _

I am aorry— very sorry," said Rebecca. "Believe me, if ever in my power, I will en- deavour to do you a kindness. but I do not wish you to sleep to-night in this house, nor do I wish Mr. Arnold Deepe under any cir- cumstances ever to visit it again." "Very well," said Mary. "I can never for- give the way you have treated me." "If you speak in that tone, please remem- ber that I can pay you your quarter's salary, and that I am not indebted to you for any. thing further." Mary looked in aurpriae at Rebecca. She had not expected this on the part of the girl. "Oh, of course," she said, "an poor and low-down folk must submit to the vagaries of the rich. Very well; I will go upstairs and pack." "You are sure I can do nothing for you?" "Nothing. May I have the cheque now ?" "I will give it to you w hen the cab is at the door, and when your boxes are on the top of the cab. Now go, please; and be quick."

div.head: CHAPTER VII.
div.p: CHAPTER VII.

When Mary Gray left the house in Pad. dock Row, where She had spent five of the most important years of her existence, she drove straight to Arnold Deepe's lodgings. There she slighted, and asked to see the landlady. The landlady's name wart Mrs. Freke. She was a round-faced, good-natured woman, and received Mary with • cheerful expres- sion in her kindly eyes. "flare you got a room in this house that you can let to me?" said Mary. "I want a bedroom and a mitting;room, land I am youpre- patoirealis..;,o rell. Mrs. was having bad times, like most of her class. wan only too pleased 1., accommodate the young lady. Mary chose the drawing-room and beilrooM behind it. Mrs. Freke named a moderate rent, and Mary agreed without demur. Was she not rich? Had she not a cheque for two hundred pounds in her miaset "I will take these rooms for • week," she said. "I cannot possibly tell whether I shall empire them longer or not. If you want re- ferences, I can give you the name of Miss Rebecca Ilenshall, 9, Paddock Row, where I hare lived as companion for the last five years." "9h, Miss," said the good landlady, ‘Mrss"lffeTs.hallragenteies etri:"Carforyomuneg Poor whose father has just died; there has been • long account of him in the 'Daily Gazette,' and a likeness, too. I always read my 'Daily (Lisette' from end to end, Miss; that's how I keep myself np to date, 80 to speak.'' Well, the old man is dead," said Mary, "and I have left Mies Hermitian, who pro- poses to make other arrangements. Will ye, have • fire lit at once in ttiis room and get me something for dinner. I want enough for two, for I expect a gentleman to dine with are this evening. Get some wine, and a bottle of whiskey. I want good wine, please- good' Burgundy-and the best Scotch whiskey. If you want money in &Nance, here's • sovereign. Have quite a nice dinner --fish, and a little joint, and something sweet, arid cheese. I am very particular, as lam accustomed to living well. I may as well tell you that I have plenty of money, no you needn't be afraid of doing your very best for me."

"I shall be only too delishted lo serve you, Miss •, and would you like linen sheets on your bed or cotton ones? I have both, Miss, but I keep the linen mostly for my drawing- room •irotors in the summer, they being colder than the cotton."

" I'll have linen sheets, " replied Mary; 'wnd please light a fire in my bedroom. By the way, you have a lodger here—Mr. Arnold Deepe " "Oh, yea, Miss. Mr. Deepe has lived with me for over two yearn. He has the top bed- sitting-room, Miss. Do you happen to know him?"

Ye,; I know him," eaid Mary. "He is the gentleman I expect to dine with me to- night." "Oh, indeed, Mimi. Well, Fee nothing to say against him." "You had better not say it, even if you have," said Mary, stoutly, "for I may as well tell you at once that I am engaged to be married to him."
Mn. Freke grew very red when Mary made thin announcement.

"I suppose I must congratulate you, Miss," she said after a pause; "but I didn't never suppose that Mr. Deepe was a marry- ing man. He seems always no set on him- self so to speak." "You know nothing about him," said Mary, with some scorn. "Now, please send your maid to make this room spiel, and span. At what hour does Mr. Deepe generally re- turn?"

"Between six and seven, an • rule. Miss; that in, tinlex, he dines out. Some days he don't dine at nil; we •II know it--that'a when he's 'ard sup. I make him a cup of cocoa then, and maybe he has • boiled egg and %nate bread and butter. Oh, he'a • qwet gentleman; I. know no harm of him, oßly somrhorr-

The woman looked at Mary with pity in her gase. Mary resented the kindly expres- sion of the good landlady's face very much indeed. When Mrs. Freke had left the room, hav- ing first put a match to the fire, Mary looked on her new surroundings. The drawing. room at No. 19, Charl”tte.street was the re- verse of inviting. Mary was accustomed to good living, to nice furniture, to the beauties which money ran put even into the simplest home. She shuddered slightly as she glanced at the dingy curtains, meant to be white, but which were in reality. • deep gray. Her

eyes fell upon the faded and very dirty 2arpet. There was a hideous paper on the walls, some pieturee of the worst typo fur- ther adorning them. There was a mirror with a cranked glass over the mantel piet,, and a round table with a ease of wan aoiers in the centre, occupying the place of howls in the room.

Mary went from the sitting-room into the bedroom, which was many degrees more gloomy, being small and dark, its windows FO covered with dirt that hut little light could pierce through. She said to herself "I cannot stand the sordidness of this for many days; but two hundred pounds can do wrinaers. Arnold and I must settle our affairs to-night. One week of three rooms will be enough for me." She ran downstairs and let herself out. ller purse was full of gold, for in addition to the cheque for two hundred pounds Rebecca whole -ter's salary: and besides, she was a :wiring creature anti had one or two five pound notes left over from her last quarter. She considered herself rich and indulged in the luxury of buying some comforts. She purchased dessert and quantities of flowers. She 41140 bought a few vases to put the flowers into and returned to her new abode about nix o'clork. . -

When she had arranged the flowers, put the awful ease of wax flowers in a dbtaut corner, pushed the hideous round table to one nide of the room, pulled forward some easy chairs and made the fire burn brightly, she looked round her with some appreciation. •.. . • .

"Arnold will be in soon now, she aunt to herself. "Bow aurpri.ed he will he to find me. I must make arrangements with him quickly. I hope Mrs. Freke will give us a decent dinner. Arnold likes good living. •• .

Mary felt no special rapture at' the thought of meeting her lover. Her feelings for him were complex. She loved him after a fashion, but not as a woman loves when her noblest and highest impulses are aroused. Six o'clock paaned Half-past six arrived. Still there was no sign of Arnold. By and by Mrs. Freke came up herself. "•-• • . . .

ten minutes tO seven, miss, and the gentleman hasn't returned. I have the din- ner cooked to a nicety. Shall I bring it up or will you wait for hinit."' By no means," mid Mary, speaking rather sharply. Have the cloth laid and have the dinner nerved at once, please." A little maid in a neat cap, hastily bought and donned for the ocemion, now appeared, put a dingy cloth on the round table, and laid mme knivea and forM and the usual paraphernalia for a meal. Mary hated the noisy, clumsy way in which the girl moved about the room. She felt inclined to snatch the things from her and lay the table hers It. She kept listening and listening for Arnold's step. Why did not he come? Presently the dinner was brought op. The girl, who announced her name an .Terninia, mid at the Asme time:

"Mr. Deepe won't be in till late to night; he'a dining at his club." Deepe invariably told the landlady on the occasions when he could afford a meal at a restaurant that he wan dining at his chib. Mary ate her solitary and unsavoury meal alone. She felt crosa and depressed. When it had come to an end she rang the bell and desired the servant to remove the dinner things. The dessert, however, remained, the wine and whiskey were on the aide table, and Mary begged for the loan of a kettle, in which she meant to boil water.

She was sitting, her hands clasped round her knees, her eyes fixed on the fire, her thoughts busy, when a quick insolent step— the step she knew no well, the step of the man she at once loved and feared, was heard. bounding up the narrow, dark stairs. Mary could not mistake it. She went immediately, flung the drawing-room door wide open, and stood where the light fell all over her. Arnold, who had let himself in, had not the least idea of her presence in the house. die started as though he new a Fhad. Then, when he realised the fact that it Warr really Mary, he entered the room, caught her in his arms and kissed her several times.

"Why, my darling!" he said, and there was genuine emotion in his voice. "What are you doing here?" "Waiting tor von, Arnold," aaid Mary. "I have plenty to tell you. Go upstairs to your room and get tidy; come down after yitimihtie, washed your hands. Have you r . .
" Yes; after a fashion."
"I had dinner waiting for you at seven o'clock. You did not come, so I ate it alone. Hut I have fruit, and biscuits and wine; you need not starve. Come down quickly, for I have much to say."

"I won't stir, said Deepe, "until I know what you are doing in these rooms." "I have taken Mrs. Freke's drawing-room floor for one week," said Mary. "This is my sitting-room; beyond is my bed-room. Now, go upstairs and come back. There ig much to talk over and arrange." Deepe gave Mary a long and wondering look. lie then turned and went up to his own room. He was absent about ten minutes. During that :ime he put on a rather shabby frock coat, brushed has black hair, and tried to make himself an presentable as he could. Ile entered Mary's room with that swinging step which she always admired. "Well," he said; "you're a plucky 'on. I am devoured with curiosity; what are you doing here?" "lo put it vulgarly," said Mary, "I re- ceived the 'sack ' from Mies Rebecca Hen- shall this morning, or rather, this afternoon. When the funeral was over she sent for me, requested me to pack, and told me that she wished to have nothing further to do with me. Sit down, please, Arnold; I have a good deal to say." "But you astound me! You have left Rebecca Henahallt"
"Mies Ilenshall, please, Arnold. It ix bad form to call • girl you hardly know by her Chrintian name."

"Oh, bother bad form!" said the man. "Mary, this is too awful. Your being out of the house upsets everything." "Well, I am out of the house, dear; and I don't at all ace how it ahould upset every- thing. If you will only sit quiet and not fidget, I will tell you my story. " Clever as Arnold Deepe was, in some ways Mary had greater ability than he. Her nature was far calmer, and in that respect she bad the upper hand of him. "Now, listen," she said. "I have told you already what occurred when I eaveadropped in the cupboard. You know well that the old man went to his account with my terrible words ringing in his ears." "You need not have said them, Mary. It was too cruel, even for my taste." "Nevertheless, I did say them, and I am glad," said Mary. "I was treated very eruelly by that family. Old Henahall and his daughter had no right to speak of me as they did."

They had every right," laughed Deepe, 'if they but knew •11. ' "But they in not know anything," answered Mary. "I therefore repeat that they had no right." "Well, my dear, acting on your advice, I only came once to the house since Henshall's death, and then I saw you quite in secret. The funeral took place to-day. Mary, I attended hut badly to my work. in the City, thinking of you, and of all that was occur- ring in Paddock Row. And now, to thid you here, and no cosy too—the whole place no home-like—l tell you it takes • fellow by storm."

Ile tried to possess himself of her hand, which she resolutely, however, kept in her lap. "If you will listen for a few minutes I selll give you certain facts. The new Homan Catholic Church of St. Thomas' of Canterbury at Centon's Green, St. Helen., woos opened on Sunday forenoon by the celebration of Pontifical I high Maio by Dr. Whiteside, Bishop of Liverpool, in the presence of Dr. Bourne, Archbishop of Westminster and Dr. Keating, Bishop of Northampton. The attend- arcs wan very large, end the service was of ea impressive character. The new church is a handsome structure of Gothic design, in rough•cut red sandstone, and has sccoromodetion for 1:00 worshippers. The intent°, is in • bit., with measive pillars of listb stone, and all the furniture is of polished pine. There are two handsome side chapels, with high alter in the main I aisle, and at the back of (i.e edifice i.e choir gallery. In attendance upon the Archbishop were Canons Pinniogton (Liverp.ol) and Connive (Prerton),deacons at the throne, and Monsigoor Jackman, D.D. ; while there were in attendance on the Bishop of Liverpool Canon Walrnaley (Liverpool), Dean O'Sullivan, and Fathers Hearne (St. Helens), deacon,Walith (Waterloo), sub-deacon, nod ClArksononaster of ceremonies, There were also present Fethere Baldwin (Holy Crow.), Ward, SJ. (Lose House), Dr. Bennett (St.. Thomas's, St. Helens), O'Mara, sal Holden. The Bishop of Northampton was the modal preacher, and gave • vivid iv:count of th• life and martyrdom of St. *Thomas of Canterbury, the patron taint of the church. _

The Archbishop of Westminster, preaching from the words," By their fruits no shall know them," said that the Cotholic Church would never allow •ov temporal advantage, any power she possessed, any influence she might acrid., to be placed in the scale neagsinst divine revelation or morality which God had entrusted to her keeping. Let them spply that same test in all charity lo those who, at the present day, outside the Catholic Church, elsimed to be the custodian, of the conscience • f men. In what he had to say, they must Oct think that he failed to appreciate the splendid reflectu, sentiment and tVe respect for religion in tho name of God and for Gin worship and for II s dinine will that he saw around them on every side In England. Let them take, first, the Established Church. Who was there to maintain that the Established Church was able to speak with divion authority on any point of rbictrine anon any contsoted point of morality in this country? That Church, despite its external p iwer, was done when there was a question of defining what God had really revealed, or of settling any contested point of morality. Take, again. those who had ...rated from the Church of England. They could take their own admistioni, [tat in many caws they were using their bold upon their people because tLey had given too much . attention to mere leocial and political problems With respect to Soctalierm his Grace said that do. content, unrest, and the uprising agsinst law, whether divine or human, were the original consequences, and therefore, the fruits o/ much of the Socialistic teach- ing. In cfAcluslon, he remarked that the Catholic Church had • great resprinsi,illty placed upon her, end eke would never cease her witness to truth and justice. div.p: IRISH AFFAIRS. NOTES FOR IRISH READERS.
THE ROW IN PARLIAMENT

We suppose that for political interest the past week has no pardlel in recent history. And to no election of the community in these islands is the supreme impost of this week's proceedings clearer than it is to the Irish people. The Constitutional crisie reached its overdue end in the publication of Mr. Asquith', letter to Mr. Balfour 31111 Lord Lansdowne and the blue blood of the self-styled superior "gentlemen of England ended up in blue funk followed by the most disgraceful treatment of the First Minister of the Crown which the annals of Parliament hold record of. Political excitement on both aides and in all parties is more or le,. inevitable on /cessions of highly important proposals being pewit into the law of the land. But the most passive and tolerant mind, British or Irish, most surely revolt at the amazing display of Parliamentary Ix oliganism which I iwered the MAhen of Parliaments from her lofty traditions t i a level beneath that of a public. house brawl. Nor is the situation mended by Mr. Balfour's audacious perversion of tho facts when is aseribrs the roardyism of his divided and defeated camp to the fact that tine Ministerial proceedings were such as to cause'• heat, and passionate heat, among the great masses of the community." Any man who has observed in however slight a degree, whether in Ilm_iland, Scotland, Wale, or Ireland, the Login features of political history during the past few years knows perfect!! well that tine /1•11016,Ileflt of Friday, illy 21st was the only logical outcome of the efforts of those years. The mannerless nobodies who yelled " Traitor "an Mr. Asquith must know in their own minds, for we suppose they have some capaci.y for trental process. that such a word might have been suggested to the men whom Mr. Aettunth has led with dignity and statesmanship had he written or spoken in terms an inch short of the p anion he took up. lie would have disappointed the great progtessive majrnity of the kingdom, he would base wrecked his party and be would have gone down to the lutist generation of history in eternal thshonour. But in all serionmes• we are told in every sheet and [screed i f the Peerw party that he has " played fast and loose with the country." And all this poet ile nonsense is scattered broadcast on every wind of the heavens because the Prime Minister Inns done what he said months sail montlia ago he would do. He has adhered to the course he ma, ped out in the sight of his countrymen , in the Albert Hall, he lons aimply given effect to the p hey upon which he and his pirty twice went to the country and were twice return.cd. We are toll he his yielded to the Irish demand. Mr. lied:snood and his party, we are informed by the sapient leader of a divided I ,pp wition, are tl.e real levies of the sit.. lion. We Irish, who were classed with the Hottentot and the brainless savages, are gratified that he should now single us out for thle distinction, but having some political memory we recall the fact that Sir Henry Cainphell.Bannerman laid down th, principles f the Veto Bill in • House of Commons where the Liberal party was aheolutely independent of the frilh vote.

div.head: CONSTITUTIONAL POSITION
div.p: THE CONSTITUTIONAL POSITION

We have no time, even if we had the inclination, t-r bandy words about the rebels and their cheap her, ice to Lord Halahury. Features of far greater import- ance mark the developments in the Tory Camp ,hiring the past few days. Alrive the din of oratory from the Smithi tea, sounds the voice of Sir William Ana m. who besides being a Conservative of the most orthodox type is easily one of the two or three greatest Constitutional experts of our day. " In all this talk of the ignominy of surrender:. says this Conservative of ex-Cabinet rank, " what Las become of the doctrine that the House of Lords has never failed to acquiesce in the decision of the electorate?" Expressing his belief thst no change in thee imposition of the House of Con-intone would result from a General Election,Sir W illliam Almon says quite frankly the Lord. will only illow accepted precedents in accepting, however rel uct a n tly "the verdict of the nation as it is now represented." This statement of the case coming as it does from a •tateraman of , Sir William Anion's standing and antecedents will I surely give e-,eiry fair and rational Unionist, for the I Cecil and Sinith type fortunately is very rare, " fan- oonly to think " as the French have it. The whole situation cannix fail to inspire greater hope into the rninda of those Irishmen who for the last three great elections here plumped solidly for the policy of democratic advance. We are nearing the fruits of those attentions fighta. And not the least helpful sign cf the hour is the hopeless division arid strife in the camp of our traditional foes, whose tactics and language Mr Birrell truly classed as belonging to the gambling hell and the thieves' kitchen.
