div.head: Mr. Harold Smith, HP, and Foreign Wire.
div.p: Mr. Harold Smith, HP, and Foreign Wire.

Sir,--As I stand ins relation to Mr. Cronfield, similar to the one that Mr. Harold Smith occupies to me, that is, not having the pleasure of his acquaint- ance, I am quite unable to say whether my declaration represents the view of Mr. Cresheld. I speak rnly for myself. And whilst Idon it fail to appreciate the inconvenit ace, and even difficulty, Which Mr. Smith, owing to his many engagements, would experience in entering upon ii "discussion tithe matter at issue. I would remind him that his proposition was made in open public meeting, and no limitation of any kind was imposed at the time. And though Ida not consider that Mr. Smith has a with to treat either myself or my argument with disrespect, I think I may claim that when a C. 30 IS put forward from a purely detached point of view, it is oftener presented in a fairer way than when the controversialist has to consider political or any other kind of expediency. The dialectic astuteiless of Mr Smith is seen when we observe that he. xpresses hie prop eition in terms of t' wire" and "tlermany," and thriehaving regard to the close and important connection r. Werra WarraNton,end the wire trade tends to introduce a bias into the argu- ment that makes a detatched and judicial examination difficult, and Mr. Smith's extranetue advantage in this respect is clear. Coming now to Mr. Rylands's letter, I have not assurntd, neither is it necessary for me to assume that the "purchase of the wire abroad necessitates the supply cf the product t,f Warrington labmir, in additioti to the supply of Warrington lab, on had the purchase of .0901.) worth of sire from outside not been made.'

The point that Ur. Rylands developes in his argu- ment is this, that as I mit of purchasing the wire abroad. the demand for commodities in Warrington would be diminished. If 11r. Rylauds can prove this. my case fails. The ry jilt is vital. let eta examine it. First of all, let us enquire where the demand for com- modities comes' from. The demand for commodities comes from lal.;our, and rothing else. If labour is lessent d the demand for comfit that's decreases ; If lab.t is Sit diminished. the demand fir commodities is not reduced. In my former lett. r, I proved that laltour or employ• mg tit in Warrington would rot Ire lessened owing to the purchase of the wire in Germany. Thereft,e Warr ing•on's dement' for ccmruodities remains una IT cc

It is undeniable that Warrimpon would have to produce goods to give in exchange for the German I wire. The production of these goods would etnp!oy Warrington labour. The employment of this labour would result in a demand for commodities, which is intro way lessened. Mr. Itylands also eft me to overlook the fact that Warrington would receive value in exchange, and that this value would be operative ix Warrinom in a similar wry to that if Warringt.'s own product. For, how cantle contend that the value of the German wire would nor be operative, when he tacitly admits that the Warring!on produce would be operative ? To ! illustrate sty point, let us assume that if the wire is made in Warrington, the wages would be ZIPS). • Then let us assume that ti.e wire is brought from Germany, and that the wages paid for the 'precinct its in Warrington of the goods t be sent in eachange,are also I,l,lfiSt. Where is the diffsrence in the purchsa- ing power of one Y.1,,50 I as compared with the other? Does it affect the grocer or clothier whether the sovereign which his customer hands over his counter has been paid by Messrs. uplands for wire-drawing or by Meows. Croslield for soammaling ? If it does not affect him, then the contention of Mr. Rylar do fails. I would ask Mr. Rylands • question, which I hope be will not consider impwtinent. Whether,from a sound commercial standpint. apart from any sentiment, he would not consider it a profitable transaction if he could buy horn Germany a quantity of material representing '2.75,0 hours of labour, that it would take his employes 3,0q0 home to produce I might add that Tariff Reformer, speak as if they could choose what to wand to the foreigner in .vchatige for his material, but I do not know of any exiting system of international etchange, bountiful or other- wise, that would eue.ble them to do so, nor can I Kay by what ' freak of barter they will be able to always send to the foreigner the product of "skilled labour " in exchange for his ' raw material." which, however, is a bait they offer to their audiences.— Yours tru'y,

- Fees for peerages and other honours are often a serious matter. There have been many cases in which a deserving man has had to refuse a title or a ribbon not only from lack of means to support it but from inability to pay the immediate fees. Perhaps the most notable instance was that of Lord Melbourne. He had the offer of the Garter more than once. On the last occasion he wrote to Queen Victoria—in 1847—that the reason why he had always avoided the honour of the Garter was because he knew that it cost LIMO, and that he had never had that amount con- veniently avaiLable.

div.head: TRAGEDY OF A DIVIDED PARTY!
div.p: THE TRAGEDY OF A DIVIDED PARTY!
WHERE STANDS MR. HAROLD SMITH, M P.? The Brothers Among the Rebels.

Recent scenes in the House of Commons and subsequent developments outside, indi- cate without the possibility of error that some of the younger and more irresponsible members of the Tory Party are in open revolt against their leaders—Lord Lans- downe and Mr. Balfour—and are willing to go to almost any lengths to save the Con- stitution."(sic.) The man who does not know when he is beaten may often compel admiration. The man who does not know how to lose decently becomes both od inus and ridiculous. The revolting Tories who refus to follow the lead of Lord Lansdowne and Mr. Balfour, when these leaders take the only constitutional course open to an Opposition which cannot furnish an alternative Govern- ment for carrying on the business of the country, have no more idea of sportsmanship than of statesmanship. In their theory of what is 'cricket,' it is ' making a gallant fight to the end " to cut up the pitch and abuse the umpire when they see that the game must be lost.

- Where has the Member for Warrington been during all these ebullitions of party loyalty and gentlemanly conduct? A very little inquiry reveals the secret—if there be any secret about it. Lord Hugh Cecil—that fanatical scion of a once noble House— and Mr. F. E. Smith, seem to have been the ringleaders in Monday's display of hooliganism, and also the moving spirits in the dinner to Lord Halsbury on Wednesday night—when the rebels dined in "the last , ditch " with so much ()chit. Among their ' chief lieutenants were Mr. Harold Smith and Lord Wolmer, the young members for ' neighbouring Lancashire constituencies which we should imagine, will think twice before they again elect the same type of representative in the House of Coot mono, Lord Wolmer has quite a close connection with the revolt, for is not his fathor, Lord Selborne, named as the possible successor to Lord Lansdowne when the ship has been scuttled and the crew done to death ? It is difficult to see what the Smith Brothers can have in view, though, may be, both possess the common weakness of humble Tories and dearly love a lord ! The Member for Warrington has not distinguished himself by taking part in the attack on the Premierffiut Ito has been very busy doing the " donkey- work " for F.E. While the latter indicted appealing epistles from Grosvenor House, Harold was busy buttonholing in the lobbies. The " Daily Chronicle " remarked on Tues- day (apropos of the Halsbury dinner) : " Desperate t from. are being made to whip ups large gathering, and this afternoon in the Lobby Mr. F. E Smith's brother and Lord Selbrirne's son wet° Iloing their utmost to dispose of tickets." The " Daily News" had been equally observant. Perpend : Finally came the desperate struggle between the opposing canvassers. Thereon the one hand was Lansdowne 11,11-e issuing its appeal for non resistance to the Parliament Bill. signed by I.rd Lansdowne. after the audience granted to him and Mr Balfour by the Sovereign On the other hand ante the brothers Smith, fulminating edicts on Grosvenor House notepaper—why, by Grosvenor House ?—and whipping nj the way, rattles for the Habilinry dinner to-niorrow. could see tl.e CinV.Su in progress—Mr. Harold Smith, with his notebook, darting this way and that as he taught sight of his prey. Before the rebels held their dinner advertising the "no surrender" movement, Mr. Balfour issued a final appeal for peace in which he referred to " the tragedy of a divided party,- and added ith Lord Lanadowne I stand with Lord Lansdowne I am ready, if need be, to fall." This appeal did not spoil the appetite of the "diners in the ditch." They were openly mutinous, and inclined to be contemptuous of Lansdowne and Balfour. The member for Warrington was present, and would doubt- less be amongst those who stood on chairs and waved table-napkins at the utterance of such fine-sounding platitudes as the following : LORD SELBORNE : The people are being robbed by the House of (Ammons of their c ;ustitutional power. P": • • • . We bel eve the HOLM of Lords to be

the ti wee, of the peple of this country. This sentiment evoked yells of delight, despite the awkward fact that the people ' elect their own House of Commons, and are prepared to dispense with the Lords. Mr. WYNDHAM volunteered the information that they were "nut indulging in heap her irs When any appexl ens made tu party loya!ty it moved him profon. dly." Oh ! these after-dinner tears ! THE DUKE OF NORTHUMBERLAND: believe the House of horde on. dnlibera live and legislative assembly in the best the world has ever peen. (Hear, hear). Doubtless—quite the best tor Dukes ! THE MARQUIS OF SALISBURY : The House of Lords is the last refuge of independence in this country." (Cheers This is merely the slobber of a Cecil ! LORD MILNER : "Let the Government appoint its own agents to do trendi work. (Auplause.)" No doubt it will---if the rebels get their own way. Mr. AUSTEN CHAMBERLAIN:

'lhe Government " haae entrapped the Crown and tleceived the people We loyal anbjeote of the comae and honest servants of the people."— Etc., etc., ad nauseam. The diners were well pleased with themselves if with no one else. It will be interesting to see how large they loom on the political horizon in the course of a week or two, when the nation has fully realised 'the depths of bounderism as "Sub Rosa" puts it---of the men who shouted down the Premier and flouted Lansdowne and Balfour in order to pose as heroes "dying in the last ditch"! Some of them could hardly die in a more suitable place !

div.head: "NO SURRENDER FIASCO.
div.p: THE "NO SURRENDER FIASCO.
Complete Collapse.

The headings are those of the " Daily Mail" which, in yesterday's issue, followed the lead of the soberer and more responsible Tory journals, and threw over the rebels, their feeble plots and foolish aspirations, wholesale. Lord Selborne, Lord Willoughby de Broke, Lord Hugh Cecil, Lord Wolmer, Mr. F. E. Smith and his brother Harold— the leaders and lieutenants in the rebellion--- must be feeling somewhat small by this. The "DAILY MAIL" sums them up as follows: The "no surrender" movement, as it Man fan- tastically on...mei!, Is already a &taco. It is perish- ing of sheer futility, and bus only euccteded in deruonetrating to a wide public what was already known to a smaller circle, namely, the p I itieal incapacity of those in whose hand* it origirated. In the beginning it had two objects (1 To serve ass demonstratioo against the leader- ship of Mr. Balfour and Lord Lansdowne : and 12 To force the GovernmeLt to prcceed to

the actual creation r f Peers, a calm which woul I have given Mr. Asquith a majority iu the Muse of Lords as well as the House of Commons. It was quickly compelled to di•avow the first object, and it now seems likely to fail in the second. All or nearly all the speakers in the dinner to Lord Halsbury, WhO Nall made the stalking horse for purpose. with which he can have hail vr ry little sympathy, paid the tribute of" respect" or" admiration." or' affecti on,- or "loyalty ' to Mr. Et Motu or Lord Lansdowne, and thus defeated the purpose for- which they were brought together, while the publica- tion of a hat of names by the Morning Pii,t "-• preetunably the most complete that could be olitainei —shows tint in actual numbers the Peers present were not sufficiently numerous to force Mr. Asquith to create a single Peer. It is true there were some Peers present who did not allow their names to be published, Ind the suppres-ion of their names can hardly be regarded as a pledge of their intention to follow Lord Ilalsbury —or Lord Selhorne—to the bitter end.

-.1:o"ni-il'illougliby de Broke, the N 1 hip of thin unborn party, yesterday refused t,, publish he names of the supporters of the "No surrender policy, and ;as we go to press we Mar that even three which he. had are being withdrawn from him. In abort the movement has collapsed. Meanwhile Lord Lansdowne bas roceived prmises- ,of support from :IS; members f the !forme of Lord.. A few comments by leading Tory papers on the scene in the Commons, and its authors, are well worth digesting. " The TIMES" says of Lord Hugh Cecil : Now that this reputation has piocurt him tho honour of representing his ruivereity, it is lamentable that he should prove a ringleader in, Parliamentary rowd ism. The" DAILY TELEGRAPH" : A colculattil and rearrangel scheme for pre- venting the Prime Mioister from gaioing • hear- ing ; the shouts of" Traitor ! "•nd hieses with which his entry was greeted ; the sheer brutality of the long-continued stream of senseless awl insolent interturi os—these things, to he frank, were simply disgusting. Such an exhibi- tion of the political unwiedom of the extremists ought to lead to the swedy collapse of whatever influence they possess. THE" BIRMINGHAM POST " : We are abet.' the Unionists who took the- unprecedented rouses of refusing a hearing to the Prime Minister did a dis-sersice to their party. Such an r xtrib lion of unmanneret hooliganism must r• lievt On the party 113 who& The (Jo' eminent Lave made themselves masters of the aisoation. The Manchester" DISPATCH." No one who has had any experience of the ways of mulct reckons the howling of a crowd at any high rate. It is not impressive, nor does it denote anything impressive. It is merely a silly display of silly temper. For if. present the battle is bet, and raving at the victors 55 senseless.
